description: Take St Peter's Basilica apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of the largest church in Christendom: from Julius II's cornerstone in 1506 to Michelangelo's dome, Bernini's baldachin and the colonnade that embraces the square.

intro: Two hundred and twenty meters long and 136.6 meters high, St Peter's Basilica took 120 years and a relay of the Renaissance's greatest architects to build. This is the story of the church at the center of the Catholic world, and of the dome, the canopy and the colonnade that made it unforgettable.
page_title: St Peter's Basilica: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: On 18 April 1506 Pope Julius II laid the cornerstone of a new St Peter's, to the design of Donato Bramante. The old Constantinian basilica, raised by Constantine the Great in the fourth century over the tomb of the apostle, was coming down, and Rome was getting the largest church in Christendom in its place. What followed was a 120-year relay through the greatest architects of the Renaissance and the Baroque: Bramante, Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, Michelangelo, Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola, Giacomo della Porta, Carlo Maderno, Gian Lorenzo Bernini and Carlo Fontana. Michelangelo, appointed chief architect in 1546, redefined the dome and gave the whole its definitive monumentality. Carlo Maderno stretched the plan into a Latin cross and raised the 114-meter facade between 1606 and 1612. Bernini, the Baroque master, set the 28.5-meter bronze baldachin over the high altar from 1624 to 1633 and later drew the colonnade that embraces the square. On 18 November 1626 Pope Urban VIII consecrated the finished basilica: 220 meters long, 150 meters wide, and built to hold some 60,000 people.
sections.heading: A 120-year building site

sections.body: Michelangelo's dome is the reason the Rome skyline looks the way it does. It rises from a drum 190 meters around and 20 meters high, reaching 73 meters above the pavement before the shell even begins. The shell itself is 42 meters across outside and 41.5 within, stiffened by sixteen ribs that converge on the lantern, with sixteen windows piercing the drum below. Above the shell come the 19-meter lantern, the 2.4-meter ball and the 4.9-meter cross: 136.6 meters from pavement to the top of the cross, still the tallest dome in the world. Giacomo della Porta raised the dome to Michelangelo's design after the master's death. Below it, four piers of 73 meters circumference each carry the weight, and their niches hold four colossal statues guarding the basilica's major relics: Bernini's St Longinus in the north-east, Andrea Bolgi's St Helena in the north-west, Francesco Mochi's St Veronica in the south-west and Francois Duquesnoy's St Andrew in the south-east.
sections.heading: The dome that crowns Rome

sections.body: Carlo Maderno's facade is 51 meters high and 114 meters wide, a giant order of columns carrying an attic with thirteen colossal statues: Christ the Redeemer at the center, St John the Baptist at his side, and the eleven apostles flanking them. Two clocks sit in the towers to either side, replacements for bell towers Bernini designed that had to come down for lack of support. On the steps below stand two 5.55-meter statues of the apostles to Rome, Peter with his keys and Paul with his sword. Five portals lead from the vestibule into the church. The northernmost is the Holy Door, walled up with bricks and opened only for holy years; the bronze door there now is Vico Consorti's work of 1950. The central portal keeps the Renaissance bronze door Antonio Averulino, called Filarete, made in 1455 for the old basilica, enlarged to fit the new space. The southernmost is the Door of the Dead, by the 20th-century sculptor Giacomo Manzu. The vestibule itself, the narthex, is 71 meters wide, 13.5 meters deep and 28 meters high, its internal pilasters a full 28 meters tall. Above the central door outside sits the Navicella, the mosaic of the ship of the Church after Giotto's design, and at the ends of the hall stand the equestrian statues: Bernini's Constantine of 1670 to the north, Cornacchini's Charlemagne to the south.
sections.heading: The facade and its five doors

sections.body: St Peter's Square is Bernini's answer to the problem of the crowd: 340 meters long and 240 meters wide, ringed by a colonnade he designed between 1656 and 1667. Each arm runs 93 meters long and 20 meters high; together the colonnade holds 284 columns, 88 pilasters and 140 statues of saints. The arms curve like the arms of the Church itself, welcoming and embracing the faithful as they stream toward the basilica. At the center stands the Vatican obelisk: 25.5 meters of red granite shaft, 40 meters in all with base and cross. It once stood in the Circus of Nero and is revered as a witness to Peter's death; in 1586 Sixtus V had Domenico Fontana move it to the square.
sections.heading: Bernini's embrace

sections.body: Under the dome, over the high altar and the tomb of St Peter below it, rises Bernini's baldachin: 28.5 meters of bronze on four helical columns 11 meters tall, built between 1624 and 1633. It marks the spiritual center of the building, the Confession where the apostle is held to lie. The nave that leads to it runs in three bays under a barrel vault 46.2 meters high, the highest church vault of its kind, framed by wide aisles and chapels. In the north aisle stands the Pieta, carved in 1498 and 1499 when Michelangelo was in his early twenties: Mary holding the dead Christ. At the far west end, the apse culminates in another Bernini ensemble holding the symbolic Chair of St Peter.
sections.heading: Under the dome

sections.body: Few buildings are as recognizable, and filmmakers know it. In Ron Howard's Angels and Demons (2009), St Peter's Square and the basilica are key locations in the hunt across Rome. The Godfather Part III (1990) includes Vatican sequences. The Two Popes (2019) tells the story of Benedict XVI and Francis against the Vatican backdrop, and Conclave (2024) sets its papal election inside the Vatican and the Sistine Chapel. Inside the basilica itself, Michelangelo's Pieta draws its own pilgrimage, and outside, Bernini's colonnade still does what it was designed to do: open its arms to the faithful. Even the obelisk has a biography: moved to the square in 1586 under Sixtus V by Domenico Fontana, it had already stood in Nero's Circus, a witness to the death of Peter.
